title: Dragon Quest: Early RPG & Engine Development
description: Dragon Quest was a personal RPG project I repeatedly rebuilt from childhood through college as my programming and graphics skills evolved. Across versions in GW-BASIC, Turing, Turbo C++, and later C++ with early DirectX and Lua scripting, it became my long-running laboratory for learning game systems, graphics, scripting, tooling, animation, and engine design.

sections.title: 1987: First Playable Version
paragraphs: I created the first version of Dragon Quest at age 12 on a Tandy 1000 EX using GW-BASIC. It was a text adventure with ASCII graphics and was complete enough for my friends to play from beginning to end.

sections.title: 1993: Complete High-School RPG
paragraphs: In high school I rebuilt Dragon Quest in Turing as a much more ambitious RPG and completed it in roughly three months for a school project.

The game played more like a traditional console RPG, with a full story, combat, character leveling, new spells, equipment purchases, secrets, explorable buildings, a castle, NPC conversations, and a final boss that required the player to become strong enough to defeat.

sections.title: Early 3D & FMV
paragraphs: I created graphics and animation using 3D Studio 4 for DOS, Deluxe Paint Animation, and graphics drawn directly in code. For the Turing version I also created pre-rendered FMV sequences in 3D Studio 4 and launched an external playback executable from the game when a movie needed to play.

sections.title: Early Sprite Rendering
paragraphs: This work predates modern PNG alpha-channel workflows. Drawing sprites with transparent backgrounds required explicit masking and raster operations rather than simply loading an image with transparency.

I remember using combinations of bitwise-style drawing operations such as AND/XOR-style masking to composite sprites, and these techniques could still be expensive on the 486-class hardware I was working with.

sections.title: Turbo C++ Rewrite
paragraphs: Sometime between the mid-1990s and 2000 I rebuilt Dragon Quest again in Turbo C++. This generation was less about finishing another story-driven RPG and more about learning how to build the underlying game technology myself.
The surviving gameplay memory is a Zelda-like exploration prototype where the player could move around the world and interact with the environment, including cutting down trees.

sections.title: 2002 C++ / DirectX Generation
paragraphs: By 2002 I had rebuilt the idea again as a Windows C++ game and engine technology demo using early DirectX-era graphics APIs. This version was intended as the technical foundation for a more mature RPG rather than a finished story-driven game.

sections.title: Lua Scripting
paragraphs: I embedded Lua into the C++ project so game behavior and cutscene logic could be driven through scripting rather than being hard-coded entirely in the engine.
The scripting layer became part of the foundation for controlling runtime behavior and experimenting with game-state changes.

sections.title: Runtime Developer Console
paragraphs: The 2002 version included a dropdown developer console inspired by the style of consoles used in games such as Doom. It exposed predefined commands that could change the running game without restarting it.
I used the console to test and manipulate systems such as weather and visual world state, including effects such as changing water into lava.

sections.title: Engine-First Development
paragraphs: The later Dragon Quest versions increasingly became engine and technology projects rather than attempts to immediately finish another RPG. I would rebuild the same basic idea whenever I learned a new language, graphics API, or architectural technique so I could understand the entire stack myself.
By the 2002 generation, most of the major foundation was present for a mature RPG framework. The major pieces I remember still missing were the final Zelda-like combat system and sound.

sections.title: Path Toward C.E.L.L.
paragraphs: Projects like Dragon Quest established the pattern that eventually led to C.E.L.L.: building reusable game technology, separating game behavior from engine internals, creating tools and scripting interfaces, and repeatedly looking for ways to make game development easier across future projects.
The technology changed dramatically over the years, but the core instinct remained the same: build the underlying systems once, then use them to make the game itself easier to create.

historicalNotes: Dragon Quest was a recurring personal game-development project that Jamie rebuilt several times from childhood through college.
The first version was created in 1987 at age 12 on a Tandy 1000 EX using GW-BASIC.
The 1987 version was a playable text adventure with ASCII graphics that Jamie's friends could play.
Jamie named his project Dragon Quest after receiving Dragon Warrior through Nintendo Power. This predates the North American Dragon Warrior series later adopting the Dragon Quest name.
The 1993 Turing version was built in roughly three months as a high-school project and was a complete playable RPG.
The high-school RPG included story, combat, leveling, spells, equipment, secrets, town and castle exploration, NPC conversations, and a final boss.
Jamie created all of the visual work himself.
Graphics were created using 3D Studio 4 for DOS, Deluxe Paint Animation, and graphics drawn directly in code.
FMV sequences were pre-rendered in 3D Studio 4 and played by shelling out from Turing to an external DOS playback executable.
Jamie remembers the external FMV player name as something similar to AAPlay, but the exact executable name is uncertain.
Early sprite transparency required explicit mask/raster operations rather than modern PNG alpha blending.
Jamie remembers AND/XOR-style compositing techniques but does not remember the exact raster-operation sequence confidently enough to document it as an exact implementation.
A later Turbo C++ rewrite was created sometime after 1995 and before 2000.
The Turbo C++ generation was primarily a technology demo rather than a complete story-driven RPG.
The strongest surviving memory of the Turbo C++ version is Zelda-like movement and environment interaction, including cutting down trees.
The 2002 generation was another fresh rewrite using C++ for Windows.
Jamie now believes the 2002 generation most likely used DirectX 5-era APIs. Exact DirectX version should be treated as memory-based rather than source-verified.
Lua was embedded into the C++ project for cutscenes and runtime scripting.
The 2002 project contained a dropdown developer console influenced by Doom-style consoles.
The console appears from surviving screenshots and memory to have exposed predefined/canned commands rather than arbitrary unrestricted Lua entry.
Runtime commands could alter systems such as weather and visual/environmental state, including changing water into lava.
The 2002 project was primarily an engine/game technology demo that could have supported a fuller story-based RPG.
Jamie remembers the main missing pieces for a more mature game being Zelda-like combat and sound.
Every Dragon Quest generation was developed solo.
These repeated personal engine and RPG projects were important conceptual predecessors to C.E.L.L.
